Because assistive technologies rely on the accessibility API mapping of role + supported states/properties to construct the accessible name, role, and value, an unsupported attribute like aria-expanded on a searchbox is either ignored or exposed inconsistently across screen readers and browsers. This breaks the WCAG 4.1.2 requirement that the role, state, and properties of a UI component be programmatically determinable, since users relying on assistive technology may not receive reliable feedback about whether the autosuggest/autocomplete list is expanded or collapsed, making the widget's behavior confusing or unusable for screen reader and voice-control users.", "severityAssessment": "Critical per axe-core's impact rating, and reasonably high-priority for WCAG 2.1 AA compliance. llmOnlyFindings.description: The image functions as a link to ca.gov, but the alt text describes it merely as 'California State Logo' rather than conveying the link's purpose/destination. Additionally, it's redundant with the adjacent screen-reader-text span 'State of California', causing duplicate announcements for screen reader users.

This image functions as a logo linking to the homepage, and it is wrapped in an anchor that already contains a screen-reader-only text 'State of California Department of Motor Vehicles' describing the destination/purpose. The img's alt text duplicates this information redundantly, causing screen reader users to hear the same content twice (once from the img alt, once from the screen-reader-text div). Per WCAG 2.4.4 (Link Purpose) and 1.1.1 (Non-text Content) best practices, when a logo is a link and adjacent text already conveys its purpose, the image's alt should either be empty (alt="") to avoid redundancy, or the redundant screen-reader-text should be removed. As currently implemented, this is a redundancy/duplication issue rather than a lack of description — the alt text itself is descriptive of the logo's content, but its coexistence with the sr-only text creates duplicate announcements for assistive technology users.

Alt text 'Five Stars' fails to convey the actual rating information the image represents (a 5-star rating graphic, likely paired with a testimonial). It doesn't specify what is being rated or that this is a visual rating indicator, which could confuse screen reader users about the image's purpose in context.

The alt text 'Five Stars' identifies the image as a graphic but fails to convey its meaning as a rating indicator. It does not communicate that this represents a 5 out of 5 star rating for the ONLINE service option, which is the actual informational content the image conveys in context.

The alt text 'Five Stars' identifies the image as a graphic but fails to convey its meaning as a rating indicator (e.g., a 5 out of 5 star rating) associated with the testimonial quote that follows. It doesn't clarify this is a rating visualization tied to the user review below it.

deepAnalysis.summary: This page shows a moderate compliance gap against WCAG 2.1 AA, with a mix of confirmed technical violations and recurring content-quality issues rather than widespread structural failure. The most urgent problem is a critical ARIA misuse on the site search input, where an unsupported aria-expanded attribute on a searchbox role breaks programmatic determinability of the autosuggest feature for screen reader and voice-control users. A second serious issue involves an inline 'Learn More' link that relies solely on insufficient color contrast to be distinguishable from surrounding text, risking that users with color blindness or low vision miss important fraud-alert information. Several moderate alt-text quality issues (redundant logo descriptions and non-descriptive 'Five Stars' rating images) add friction for assistive technology users but are lower priority. Given this appears to be a government (DMV) portal likely subject to ADA Title II and Section 508 requirements, and includes a well-documented, easily-flagged violation (1.4.1) tied to consumer-protection content, there is meaningful legal exposure that warrants prompt remediation of the critical and serious findings.
